doc.title: Ellis Marsalis — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: The Monk CD and its selections
summary: Marsalis describes An Open Letter to Thelonious, with Jason and the selections.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk

blocks.x: Okay. I’d like to ask you, since I was just talking with Bobby Jackson, who’s in Cleveland, a radio personality, and he shared with me that he had written some notes about your current release, a CD release, a feature of Monk material. I just wondered if you’d like to talk about that as being your most recent recording.

The open invitation to Thelonious, which is the title of the CD [An Open Letter to Thelonious] was conceptualized primarily by Jason. He was thinking that a lot of what Monk would work very good with some more – I don’t want to say funk drums, because it’s not straight up, but more liberal approaches to the drum set and the way that he envisioned it to be.

I had been working at Snug Harbor with Jason and a saxophonist named Derek Douget and a bass player named Jason Stewart. Eventually, they left. Jason left basically to do his own thing. Stewart went up to New York. In fact, he’s in that two-year program at the Juilliard. He’s studying with Ron Carter. The saxophonist got married, left town, and he’s back. We just started hooking up since he’s come back, but we went in the studio and recorded five or six – I forgot how many now – of Monk’s compositions.
Who chose the selections? Jason? Or yourself? Or was it a group decision?

It was a combination of things. I did – I think I did ’Round Midnight. It was solo. I think, anyway. Some of the pieces – Jackie-ing was definitely Jason’s decision, and Teo was also Jason’s decision. I had arranged, in a way, Monk’s Mood, whenever possible just using what Monk did, Monk’s voicings, Monk’s chords. I had done a transcription a while back of Crepuscule with Nellie. So we recorded that. We did Epistrophy, and Straight No Chaser in the right key.
Meaning which?
Meaning not following the mis-directions of Miles Davis, who played it in the wrong key.
The right key being?
B-flat.
Got it. Why did Miles change it? Do you know?
Yeah, it’s easier to play on the trumpet in some of them other keys Miles changed the keys to.
Straight No Chaser. Okay. The first two selections you mentioned, were those arranged by Jason, since you mentioned that you arranged most of the others?
I forgot what the first two are? Was it Jackie-ing?
Uh-huh.
Basically, what we did was to play the head just the way Monk played it. Basically that. So I think Jackie-ing – that’s a real tricky song anyway – and whatever was the other one that I said.
Teo [Tee-oh].
Oh, Teo [Tay-oh]. Right.
Excuse me. Teo Macero.
We did basically the same thing that Monk did. Crepuscule, we just used that transcription that I did, because Crepuscule doesn’t have any solo in it.
Right. Through composed.
We added a little on Monk’s Mood at the very end.
